clue.text: Crew on board trendy vessel

indicators.note: being on board a vessel means being inside it, between the two letters that abbreviate a powered ship

parts.note: SS is the standard prefix for a steam-powered vessel, and the crew goes between its two letters
a crew is a team working together
hip means fashionable

explanation.surface: Sailors aboard a fashionable boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' does double duty: it puts the crew inside SS, the standard abbreviation for steamship, before HIP is added on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A steamship is a large boat driven by steam engines, one kind of seagoing craft.

clue.text: Clue for Poles to leave discreetly

parts.note: surface reading: a hint written for people from Poland
setter's reading: the answer is itself a tiny clue whose first word is a jumble of the nationality, with the second word as its signal to rearrange

explanation.surface: A crossword hint aimed at Polish solvers, who should then quietly slip away.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: read the answer as a clue in its own right, SLOPE with OFF as an anagram signal, and it produces POLES.
explanation.definitionFit: To slope off is a colloquial phrase for sneaking away quietly without being noticed.

clue.text: Fixed rate including unknown bonus

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece goes within another
something fixed has been repaired or rigged, so the letters are put right in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
X is the classic algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A fixed pay rate that comes with a mystery bonus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixed rate' reads as a financial term, but 'Fixed' is the signal to rearrange RATE before X is slotted in.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra is something additional given on top of what is expected, just like a bonus payment.

clue.text: Parliamentarian hit hopeless problem with hellish character

parts.note: MEP is a Member of the European Parliament

indicators.note: a problem is something gone wrong, so the letters are in a troubled state needing rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician runs into a hopeless difficulty involving a devilish person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hit' looks like a verb for the politician's action, but it is just anagram fodder alongside 'hopeless'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mephistopheles is the demon of the Faust legend who bargains for souls, a figure straight out of hell.

clue.text: After stripping, they raved: the cop delivered marching orders

indicators.note: stripping peels off the outer layer, so each word loses its outside letters and keeps its core

parts.note: the inner part of the first word
the inner part of the second word
the inner letter of the third word
the inner letter of the fourth word

explanation.surface: After a strip show, partygoers went wild and a police officer told them to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stripping' suggests a striptease, but here it means removing the first and last letter of each of the four words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving someone the heave-ho is an informal idiom for dismissing them, the same as handing out marching orders.

clue.text: Fancy lady in dance up for modelling stuff

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards
one thing in another sits inside it

parts.note: a hop is an informal dance

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or imaginative, so the letters take on a decorative new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A glamorous woman at a dance is ready to pose as an artist's model.
explanation.walkthrough: A hop is an old word for a dance; it is reversed to POH and the rearranged LADY goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Play-Doh is a brand of soft coloured dough that children shape into models.

clue.text: Anyhow, let's abandon obsolete instrument

indicators.note: anyhow means in any old way, carelessly, so the letters come in no fixed order
to abandon is to leave behind, so these letters are dropped

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe
taken as written

explanation.surface: A call to give up on an out-of-date musical instrument anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: The four letters to remove from 'obsolete' are those of 'let's' scattered through it, not in that order, hence 'Anyhow'.
explanation.definitionFit: The oboe is a double-reed woodwind played in orchestras.

clue.text: Left cattle covered by BBC3

definitions.note: a cross-reference: the answer to 3 down, a devilish figure

indicators.note: something covered by another is wrapped inside it

parts.note: the Beeb is the British nickname for the BBC, the national broadcaster
L is the abbreviation for left
the zebu is a humped breed of cattle

explanation.surface: Leftover livestock coverage on the TV channel BBC Three.
explanation.walkthrough: 'BBC3' looks like the channel name, but it splits: BBC gives the Beeb and the 3 points to 3 down for the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Beelzebub is a name for the Devil or a chief demon, just as the earlier hellish character is.

clue.text: Contemporary top navigation instrument

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: a sextant measures angles between stars and the horizon for navigation

explanation.surface: A state-of-the-art, first-rate tool for finding your way at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' reads as an adjective meaning best, but it is a verb here: behead the instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Extant means still existing today, so something extant belongs to the present time.

clue.text: Control supporting bonds as they provide strength

parts.note: to rein in is to control
if you are for something you support it
to cement is to bond firmly

explanation.surface: A note on structural engineering: restraint holding bonds together gives strength.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bonds' looks like a noun but is a verb, matching 'cements'.
explanation.definitionFit: Reinforcements are extra troops or supports that make a force or structure stronger.

clue.text: Some don't appear available

indicators.note: some means only a part, so the letters are a portion of the following words

parts.note: runs across the two words, skipping the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A few people fail to turn up when they are supposed to be free.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through 'don't appear', with the apostrophe ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: On tap is an idiom for ready whenever needed, like beer drawn from a barrel.

clue.text: A tendency to conceal same but different disgrace

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: concealing something means hiding it inside something else

parts.note: a bent is a natural inclination

indicators.note: made different means changed in form, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A habit of covering up an embarrassment that is the same yet somehow different.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Same but different' sounds like a catchphrase, but 'same' is the fodder and 'different' its signal, hidden inside A BENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Abasement is humiliation or a lowering of dignity, which is what disgrace brings.

clue.text: Except when reversing, I have become deceitful

indicators.note: reversing means going backwards, so this word is read the other way round

parts.note: save is an old word meaning except, as in 'all save one'
the contraction I've

explanation.surface: A confession that, apart from in reverse gear, the speaker has turned dishonest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Except' meaning 'save' is the leap needed; the reversed word then joins the contraction I've.
explanation.definitionFit: An evasive person dodges straight answers, which is a shifty, misleading way of behaving.

clue.text: Study one form of Buddhism as resident

parts.note: a den is a private study room
Roman numeral one
Zen is a school of Buddhism

explanation.surface: Someone takes up a Buddhist practice while living somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' reads as a verb, but it is the room, DEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A denizen is an inhabitant or occupant of a particular place.

clue.text: Nitpicker finding lie about cotton, home-spun

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: a fib is a small lie

indicators.note: spinning turns things round and round, so the letters are churned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A pedant discovers a falsehood about home-spun cotton cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home-spun' looks like one adjective, but the hyphen hides 'home' as fodder and 'spun' as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A comb with tightly set teeth literally picks lice eggs out of hair, and also stands for meticulous scrutiny.

clue.text: Mustang sound and smell extremely unfamiliar for local resident

parts.note: a mustang is a wild horse, and a horse's call is a neigh
BO is body odour

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremes, the two ends of a word

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: A horse's noise and an odd smell are reported by someone living nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: BO for body odour is a crossword favourite; the horse call supplies the opening.
explanation.definitionFit: A neighbour is a person living next door or close by, so someone resident in the locality.

clue.text: The Guardian, for one, rose over for this howler

parts.note: a newspaper editorial speaks of itself as 'we'

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: a rose is a flower

explanation.surface: The newspaper climbed over itself to cover a glaring mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like a verb, but it is the flower; 'howler' looks like a blunder, a favourite misdirection for this setter's own paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A werewolf is a mythical person turned wolf that howls at the full moon.

clue.text: Unrealistic start of play by awfully prim conductor

indicators.note: awfully means badly, so the letters are in a terrible jumble

parts.note: taken as written
Act I opens a stage play
a cable conducts electricity

explanation.surface: A fanciful opening to a show, put on by a very prissy orchestra leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' suggests a musician, but it is an electrical one; 'by' means next to, so the anagram precedes the opening act.
explanation.definitionFit: Impracticable means not able to be done in practice, so the plan is not realistic.

clue.text: A timeless relative essential in surgery

indicators.note: less means without, and time is abbreviated to one letter, so that letter goes

parts.note: taken as written
a stepsis is a stepsister, a relative by marriage

explanation.surface: A family member who never ages is vital in an operating theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: T is the standard abbreviation for time; drop it from the informal stepsis and put A in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Asepsis is the absence of germs in a sterile environment, which operations require.

clue.text: Starts eating food with greed?

parts.note: tuck is British slang for food, especially snacks at school
greed is one of the seven deadly sins

explanation.surface: Someone digs into a meal greedily.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that greed stands for its category, a deadly sin.
explanation.definitionFit: To tuck in is an informal phrase for beginning a meal heartily.

clue.text: Kind of treatment for computer

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a pill taken as medicine
second meaning: a flat touchscreen device

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests repairing a computer, but the pill and the device are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A tablet is a compressed pill of medicine and also a slim handheld touchscreen computing device.

clue.text: Sportsperson's permit to enter articles

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: A and THE are the indefinite and definite articles
to let is to permit

explanation.surface: A sports star's pass to get into the press stories.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay; 'articles' are the grammatical ones, not newspaper pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An athlete is someone who competes in sport, especially running and field events.

clue.text: Write regularly cool and fancy poems

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

parts.note: alternate letters: the odd ones, first and third

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate, so the letters are dressed up in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to produce verse often, both cool and ornate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' looks like advice on how often to write, but it trims 'cool' to its odd letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To compose is to create a piece of music or literature, putting it down on paper.

clue.text: On coronary care units resuscitation starts to take place

indicators.note: starts are beginnings, so the opening letter of each word is taken

parts.note: initial letters of five words

explanation.surface: On hospital heart wards, revival efforts begin to happen.
explanation.walkthrough: The medical scene hides an acrostic of the first five words.
explanation.definitionFit: To occur means to happen, an event coming about at a given time.

clue.text: Remarkably noiseless football players

indicators.note: remarkably means strikingly unusual, so the letters are put in an unusual order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A team of footballers who play surprisingly quietly.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lionesses is the nickname of the England women's football team, European champions in 2022.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of England's women's national football side are known collectively by this big-cat nickname.

clue.text: From kitchen, a chocolate snack

indicators.note: from means taken out of, so the letters are lifted directly from the words that follow

parts.note: runs across three words

explanation.surface: A sweet treat fetched from the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: The chocolate leads towards a sweet, but the snack is savoury and spans the end of 'kitchen' to the start of 'chocolate'.
explanation.definitionFit: A nacho is a tortilla chip, usually served with melted cheese, eaten as a light bite.

clue.text: They reinforce walls of old city

indicators.note: walls are the outer edges, so only the outside letters of each word are kept

parts.note: first and last letters
first and last letters

explanation.surface: People shoring up the fortifications of an ancient town.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pulls towards the car part, since a tyre has reinforced sidewalls, but the definition is the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyre was an ancient Phoenician port on the coast of present-day Lebanon.

clue.text: Spam? Nosh oddly backfires and can be grotesque

indicators.note: oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, so the first, third and so on are kept

parts.note: odd letters, ignoring the question mark

indicators.note: back means backwards, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: the word after its first four letters, which serve as the signal

explanation.surface: Tinned meat as dinner goes badly wrong and looks monstrous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backfires' splits into a reversal signal and its fodder; 'grotesque' is not ugly here but a name for a family of typefaces.
explanation.definitionFit: Grotesque is the printers' term for an early style of typeface without serifs, one kind of plain lettering.
